Let me analyze this OIML certificate markdown.

Certificate details:

- Project number: 1901388
- Pages: 3
- Member state: The Netherlands
- Date issued: 28 August 2017
- Issuing authority: NMi Certin B.V., OIML Issuing Authority NL1
- Person responsible: C. Oosterman, Head Certification Board
- Address: Hugo de Grootplein 1, 3314 EG Dordrecht, the Netherlands
- Phone: +31 78 6332332
- Email: certin@nmi.nl
- Website: www.nmi.nl
- oiml_issuer_id: NL1

Applicant and Manufacturer: Mettler-Toledo (Changzhou) Measurement Technology Ltd., 111, West Taihu Road, XinBei District, Changzhou, Jiangsu, 213125, P.R. of China

Certified type: Indicator, types IND245 / IND246

Recommendation: R76-1, Edition 2006, accuracy classes (III), (IIII), scheme... The scheme field in recommendation: scheme (A|B) at certificate level. Hmm, "scheme (A|B)" — OIML-CS has Scheme A and Scheme B. The certificate doesn't explicitly mention scheme. Hmm. NMi certificates are typically Scheme A? Actually the OIML-CS basic system has scheme A (certificate issued based on full evaluation by issuing authority) and scheme B (based on manufacturer's declaration + type evaluation report review). The markdown doesn't state scheme explicitly. Rule 8: don't fabricate. But the schema says certificate.scheme is (A|B). Since it's not stated, I could omit it. Hmm, but it's in the schema... The instructions say "If a field is not present in the markdown, omit it." So omit scheme. Actually wait — many NMi certs are scheme A. But not stated here. I'll omit it to be safe.

Test reports:
- No. 11200016-01 dated 18 May 2011, 47 pages, role: type_evaluation_report (OIML Test Report)
- No. 11200016-02 dated 18 May 2011, 38 pages
- No. 11200016-03 dated 18 May 2011, 13 pages
- No. 13200507-01 dated 6 November 2013, 27 pages
- No. NMi-15200477-01 dated 29 October 2015, 7 pages

All are OIML Test Report(s), role type_evaluation_report.

Revision history:
- Revision "Initial", date 10 November 2015, changes "-"
- Revision "1", date 8 August 2017, "Software identification corrected."
- Revision "2", date 28 August 2017, "Typing error in issuing date and date in certificate history"

Characteristics — Type level (indicator):
- accuracy_class: "(III) and (IIII)" — hmm, values. Accuracy classes: III, IIII. I could represent as a list? The structured value rules say lists of values are model matrix... but for accuracy class at recommendation level we have accuracy_classes: ["III", "IIII"]. For characteristics, maybe accuracy_class value as string "(III) and (IIII)"? Hmm. Let me think. Perhaps put accuracy_classes in recommendation only, and skip characteristics.accuracy_class or represent as type_level with value string "III", "IIII"? I'll include a type_level characteristic accuracy_class with value ["III", "IIII"]? No — value must be number, {min,max}, or string. I could do value: "III, IIII"? That's odd. Maybe better to put in recommendation.accuracy_classes and not in characteristics. But the characteristics table explicitly lists "Accuracy class: (III) and (IIII)". I could encode as type_level: accuracy_class: {value: "III and IIII"}... Hmm.

Alternatively, since weighing ranges include Single interval / Multi-interval / Multiple range, these are different variants... but they aren't tied to IND245 vs IND246 explicitly. The certificate covers two types IND245 and IND246.

Weighing ranges: Single interval, Multi-interval, Multiple range — these are supported configurations (string values). I'd encode as type_level: weighing_ranges: {value: "Single interval, Multi-interval, Multiple range"}? Or as a list-as-string. Hmm. Could also treat as separate booleans. I'll keep as a string list value.

Power supply: 100-240 V AC 50/60 Hz or 7.2 V (NiMH battery). Per rule 3, split:
- power_supply_voltage: {min: 100, max: 240}, unit V — but also battery 7.2 V DC. Hmm. Two alternatives: AC mains 100-240 V, or battery 7.2 V. Maybe encode:
  - power_supply_voltage_ac: {min:100, max:240} V
  - power_supply_voltage_battery: 7.2 V (note decimal comma converted from 7,2)
  - power_supply_type: "AC or DC battery (NiMH)"
  
Let me structure:
- power_supply_voltage: {value: {min: 100, max: 240}, unit_symbol: "V"} — for AC mains
- power_supply_frequency: {min:50, max:60} Hz
- power_supply_type: "AC" ... plus battery alternative. Maybe add: battery_voltage: 7.2 V, battery_type: "NiMH".

Temperature range: -10 °C / +40 °C → {min: -10, max: 40}, °C.

Maximum number of load platforms: 1.

Application: "Intended to be used for direct sales to the public" — string.

Analog load cell config (config_level? or components section?). The schema has config_level for attribute × config-axis matrix. Here we have two configuration axes: analog load cell connection and digital load cell connection. Attributes vary by config:

If analog load cell(s):
- max verification scale intervals: 6000 (analog) vs 10000 (digital)
- fraction of maximum permissible error: 0.5 (analog) vs 0 (digital)
- load cell excitation voltage: 5 V DC or 10 V DC (analog only) — two columns: 5 V DC → 0.83 µV min input voltage; 10 V DC → 1 µV. This is a config axis: excitation voltage.
- minimum load cell resistance: battery version 87 Ω; AC mains version 43 Ω (analog only)
- maximum load cell resistance: 1200 Ω (analog only)
- max cable length: 4-wire: direct connection; 6-wire: no special cable length
- software identification: analog: ID 72257764, version 1.xx; digital: ID 30065264, version 2.xx.yyyy

Hmm wait — actually the software identification differs between analog and digital sections. Interesting: analog → 72257764 v1.xx; digital → 30065264 v2.xx.yyyy. This is config-level.

So config_level entries with axis "load_cell_type" (analog vs digital):

- attribute: max_verification_scale_intervals, axis: load_cell_connection
  - condition: analog load cell, value 6000
  - condition: digital load cell, value 10000
- attribute: fraction_of_maximum_permissible_error (plc-like, apportionment factor)
  - analog: 0.5
  - digital: 0
- attribute: load_cell_excitation_voltage, analog only: 5 V DC OR 10 V DC. Two columns: excitation 5V → min input voltage 0.83 µV; excitation 10V → 1 µV. This could be config axis "load_cell_excitation_voltage" for attribute "minimum_input_voltage_per_verification_scale_interval".
- attribute: minimum_load_cell_resistance, axis: power supply version: battery → 87 Ω, AC mains → 43 Ω (analog only)
- maximum_load_cell_resistance: 1200 Ω (analog only) — type_level? It only applies in analog config. Put in config_level with axis load_cell_connection, condition analog, value 1200 Ω.
- max cable length: 4-wire → "Direct connection"; 6-wire (remote sensing) → "No special cable length". Axis: cable_type.
- software_identification_number: analog 72257764, digital 30065264
- software_version: analog "1.xx (xx between 0 and 99)", digital "2.xx.yyyy"

Also model level? The two types IND245 and IND246 — do characteristics vary per model? Not specified; characteristics apply to both. So models IND245, IND246 in model_family? Rule 4 says model_family include ONLY if cert covers >1 model variant. Here there are two types IND245/IND246 with same characteristics. Hmm — is it a "family"? The certified_type.type_designations would include both IND245 and IND246. model_family is for variants where attributes vary per model. Since no attribute varies between IND245 and IND246, maybe omit model_family and just list type_designations. I think that's cleaner: type_designations: ["IND245", "IND246"], no model_family.

Now config_level structure per schema:
```
config_level[]:
  attribute, axis, values[]: {condition, value}
```
Values follow structured form: {condition, value, unit_symbol}. So each value object: {condition: "analog load cell", value: 6000}. With unit_symbol and unit_id and footnote_markers presumably.

Let me draft config_level entries:

1. attribute: "max_verification_scale_intervals", axis: "load_cell_type"
   values: [{condition: "analog load cell(s)", value: 6000}, {condition: "digital load cell(s)", value: 10000}]

2. attribute: "fraction_of_maximum_permissible_error", axis: "load_cell_type"
   values: [{condition: "analog load cell(s)", value: 0.5}, {condition: "digital load cell(s)", value: 0}]
   
Hmm, fraction 0 for digital — 0? That's what the table says: "Fraction of the maximum permissible error: 0". Interesting, but that's what it says. Actually wait — maybe it's "0.5" and OCR dropped ".5"? The markdown says "0". Rule 8: don't fabricate; extract as given. Value 0.

3. attribute: "load_cell_excitation_voltage", axis: "load_cell_type", analog only:
   values: [{condition: "analog load cell(s)", value: 5, unit_symbol: "V"}, ...]? But there are two options 5 V DC or 10 V DC. And these correspond to min input voltage columns. Better: config axis = excitation voltage, attribute = minimum_input_voltage_per_verification_scale_interval:
   - attribute: "minimum_input_voltage_per_verification_scale_interval", axis: "load_cell_excitation_voltage"
     values: [{condition: "5 V DC", value: 0.83, unit_symbol: "µV"}, {condition: "10 V DC", value: 1, unit_symbol: "µV"}]
   And separately load_cell_excitation_voltage as type-level? It's analog-only. Could add config_level attribute load_cell_excitation_voltage axis load_cell_type with values [{condition: "analog load cell(s)", value: "5 V DC or 10 V DC"}]. Hmm, value "5 V DC or 10 V DC" as string. Or two entries with same condition: value 5 and value 10 — but structured value is single. I'd encode excitation voltage as a config_level entry with axis "load_cell_type" and condition "analog load cell(s)", value: {min:5, max:10}? No — those are alternatives, not a range. Keep as string "5 or 10", unit "V DC"? Hmm.

   Alternative: keep it simple: value string "5 V DC or 10 V DC" with unit_symbol null. I'll do: {condition: "analog load cell(s)", value: "5 or 10", unit_symbol: "V DC"}. Hmm, "V DC" as unit_symbol is a bit odd but acceptable? Rule says leave unit_id null unless certain; unit_symbol can be raw. Maybe unit_symbol "V" and note DC in condition? I'll do value "5 or 10", unit_symbol "V DC". Actually cleaner: two separate characteristics? Let me just encode:
   
   - attribute: "load_cell_excitation_voltage", axis: "load_cell_type", values: [{condition: "analog load cell(s)", value: "5 or 10", unit_symbol: "V DC"}]

4. minimum_load_cell_resistance, axis: "power_supply" (analog only):
   values: [{condition: "battery version (analog)", value: 87, unit_symbol: "Ω"}, {condition: "AC mains version (analog)", value: 43, unit_symbol: "Ω"}]
   Conditions could reference both axes: analog + battery/AC. I'll write condition "analog load cell(s), battery version" etc.

5. maximum_load_cell_resistance: analog only, 1200 Ω. config_level axis load_cell_type condition analog.

6. maximum_cable_length_per_cross_wire_section... The value cells are "Direct connection" and "No special cable length" — strings, not numeric. attribute: "max_cable_length_indicator_to_junction_box_or_load_cells", axis: "cable_type", values: [{condition: "4-wire", value: "Direct connection"}, {condition: "6-wire (remote sensing)", value: "No special cable length"}]. These are strings; fine.

7. software_identification_number, axis "load_cell_type": analog 72257764, digital 30065264.

8. software_version, axis "load_cell_type": analog "1.xx (xx = 0..99)", digital "2.xx.yyyy (xx = 00..99, yyyy = 0000..9999)". Keep as strings.

Type level:
- accuracy_class: value "III", "IIII" — hmm. I'll put recommendation.accuracy_classes: ["III", "IIII"]. And maybe type_level accuracy_class: {value: "III, IIII"}? To avoid duplication weirdness, I might skip in characteristics. But the characteristics table lists it. I'll include type_level accuracy_class with value string "(III) and (IIII)"? Hmm, "(III)" parentheses are notation for class III. I'd use "III and IIII". Let me include: {"accuracy_class": {"value": "III and IIII"}}? The value must be number|{min,max}|string. OK.

Actually maybe better: since accuracy class applies to whole cert, recommendation.accuracy_classes covers it. But being faithful, I'll include both. I'll set type_level accuracy_class value "III" and "IIII"... can't. I'll go with string "III, IIII".

Hmm, let me reconsider: schema example for recommendation includes accuracy_classes[]. So that's the canonical place. I'll include it there and also as type_level characteristic for fidelity. Fine.

- weighing_ranges: value: "Single interval, Multi-interval, Multiple range" (string). Or encode as three separate? I'll do a single string.

- temperature_range: {min: -10, max: 40}, unit °C.

- max_number_of_load_platforms: 1.

- application: "Intended to be used for direct sales to the public" (string).

Also power supply split as discussed:
- power_supply_voltage: {min:100, max:240} V
- power_supply_frequency: {min:50, max:60} Hz
- power_supply_type: "AC" (mains) — plus battery alternative. Add:
- battery_supply_voltage: 7.2 V (converted from 7,2)
- battery_type: "NiMH"

There's revision_history array. I could add certificate field... schema doesn't have "revision" field at cert level. Hmm, revision_history includes rev 2 with date. I'll just use number without revision. Or number "R76/2006-NL1-15.49" and keep revision_history. Good.

The certificate says R76-1 Edition 2006. Schema: id (canonical e.g. "R60"), edition (int), amendment, scheme, accuracy_classes. There's no "part" field. I could set id "R76" and edition 2006. Part info lost, but maybe include in id? "R76-1"? The rule says canonical e.g. "R60" not "OIML R 60". So id "R76". Hmm, but part matters. I could set id "R76-1"? That deviates from canonical "R76". I think "R76" with edition 2006 is fine; maybe mention part in a description? There's no field. I'll use id "R76", edition 2006. Actually, maybe better to preserve: id: "R76", edition: 2006. model_family: Since two types IND245/IND246 but no per-model varying attributes, I'll omit model_family per "include ONLY if cert covers >1 model variant" — hmm, it does cover 2 models. Including model_family with models [{model_id: "IND245"}, {model_id: "IND246"}] and no model_level characteristics seems reasonable and harmless. The rule: "include ONLY if cert covers >1 model variant". The cert covers 2 types. I'll include model_family with family_name null and both models. To be precise, conditions: "analog load cell(s) – battery version", "analog load cell(s) – AC mains version".

5. maximum_load_cell_resistance, axis: "load_cell_type", values: [{condition: "analog load cell(s)", value: 1200, unit_symbol: "Ω"}]

6. max_cable_length... axis: "cable_connection", values: [{condition: "4-wire", value: "Direct connection"}, {condition: "6-wire (remote sensing)", value: "No special cable length"}]. This applies to analog connection too (between indicator and junction box or load cells). Attribute name: "maximum_cable_length_per_cross_wire_section_indicator_to_junction_box_or_load_cells" — long. Maybe "max_cable_length_per_cross_wire_section". Values are strings, so it's descriptive rather than numeric. Fine.

7. software_identification_number, axis: "load_cell_type": analog 72257764, digital 30065264.

8. software_version, axis: "load_cell_type": analog "1.xx (xx = 0–99)", digital "2.xx.yyyy (xx = 00–99, yyyy = 0000–9999)". Use strings without en-dash maybe: "1.xx where xx is 0-99". Keep as "1.xx (xx between 0 and 99)" and "2.xx.yyyy (xx between 00 and 99, yyyy between 0000 and 9999)".

Value objects in config_level: schema says values[]: {condition, value} and rule 5 says values follow the same structured form {condition, value, unit_symbol}. I'll include unit_symbol, unit_id: null, footnote_markers omitted/empty. For string values, unit_symbol null.

Should numeric values include unit_id? Rule: leave null unless certain. I could include unitsdb ids for common ones: u:degree_Celsius, u:volt, u:hertz, u:ohm, u:microvolt... but "Leave unit_id: null unless you are certain". I'm reasonably certain of degree_Celsius and volt... but to be safe, I'll leave null for all, providing unit_symbol only. Actually the example shows "u:degree_Celsius" as a possibility. I'll set null everywhere to avoid wrong IDs.
